walkthroughs.body_html:
Paper 2: Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives — a core area of GCSE English Language.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Paper 2: Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Paper 2: Writers' Viewpoints and Perspectives.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Standard English is the original and correct form of the language.
A dialect that has gained social and institutional prestige — used in education and formal writing; it is one variety, not inherently superior in linguistic terms.
Standard English is the same as Received Pronunciation.
A noun phrase is a sentence that contains nouns.

mcqs.q: What is a speech act according to Searle/Austin?
options: A speech act is a performance or a play.
Standard English is the same as Received Pronunciation.
An utterance that performs an action — promising, ordering, apologising, declaring. Speech acts have locutionary (what's said), illocutionary (intended force) and perlocutionary (effect) dimensions.
A speech act is any time someone speaks.
A syntactic unit headed by a noun, which may include determiners, adjectives and modifiers — e.g. 'the big red car' is a noun phrase functioning as a single grammatical unit.
Standard English is the same as Received Pronunciation.
A noun phrase is a sentence that contains nouns.
A noun phrase is just a noun by itself.
